lede: Brazil picks its president today in a runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro that polls call a coin flip.
The US is moving forces into the Middle East amid planning for a possible new strike on Iran, which keeps oil, and therefore Aussie inflation, in play.
This week decides the next RBA move: September quarter CPI lands Thursday, with the cash rate already at 4.60% and the RBA meeting on Melbourne Cup day.

stories.h: Brazil votes in a knife edge runoff today
stories.b: President Lula, 80 and chasing a fourth term, faces Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro. Flávio surprisingly topped the first round on 4 October, and the first Datafolha poll after it had him on 49% to Lula's 45%, which is still a statistical tie.
stories.w: Brazil is Latin America's biggest economy and a major commodity exporter competing with Australia in iron ore and beef. A Bolsonaro win would also add another Trump aligned leader to the G20.

stories.h: US and Israel weigh a fresh strike on Iran
stories.b: Military reinforcements are heading to the Middle East and the US has ordered nonessential diplomats out of Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks. This follows a year of conflict that began with the 28 February US and Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Khamenei and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.w: Oil is the transmission line to your wallet. Brent hit about US$109 in September, and Australia imports most of its refined fuel, so Middle East escalation feeds straight into petrol prices, CPI and RBA decisions.

stories.b: Trump waived the Russia sanctions in a bill Congress passed overwhelmingly, agreed a diesel deal with Moscow, and said it was time for someone else to negotiate for Ukraine. Kyiv also lost more than a week of normal Starlink service for its drones before speeds were restored on Friday.
stories.w: This is a sharp reversal from July, when Trump backed Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries. Europe now carries more of the burden, which is why defence spending is rising almost everywhere.

stories.h: Israel holds its first election since 7 October 2023
stories.b: Israelis vote on Tuesday 27 October. Tensions are high in the occupied West Bank, where Israel ordered a closure on Friday after soldiers killed two men accused of an attack near Hebron.
stories.w: The result could reset Israel's approach to Gaza, Iran and its relationships with Gulf states and the US.

quick.x: Ebola has spread from Congo, with Nigeria and Kenya recording their first cases of the current outbreak.
Bulgaria also holds a presidential election today, with a runoff on 1 November if needed.
US midterms are on 3 November and millions of Americans have already voted early.
New Zealand goes to the polls on 7 November, with Labour and National tied in recent polling.

stories.h: AI found a bug that exposes about 70% of websites
stories.b: Researchers at Calif and Google's Wiz used frontier AI models to find PHP2Shell, a set of flaws in the PHP language that let attackers run code on a server. Some of the bugs had been hidden for over a decade. Patches dropped on 21 October and the NSA told organisations to patch immediately or go offline. Exploit attempts are already climbing.
stories.w: It is being compared to Heartbleed. The bigger story is that AI now finds and weaponises old bugs in days, which helps defenders and attackers equally.

stories.b: China's DeepSeek is reportedly close to a US$15 billion funding round, and Meta posted US$64.6 billion in quarterly revenue. Meta also now charges Facebook Pages to post more than two links a month, a sign platforms want to keep you inside the app.
stories.w: AI investment is a large reason global interest rates and borrowing costs are staying high, according to BlackRock's risk tracking.

stories.h: AI is starting to show up in layoffs
stories.b: A Reuters tally counts 31 companies that have linked 102,800 job cuts to AI since October 2025, with banks making up 39% of them.
stories.w: NAB's 2,500 job cuts this week (see Business) fit the same pattern of banks automating back office work.

stories.h: Military AI is causing friction inside Big Tech
stories.b: Google DeepMind researchers have resigned over contracts with US and Israeli forces, and a US congressional watchdog found the Pentagon does not always follow its own responsible AI rules.
stories.w: Expect AI in defence to become a bigger political issue, including for Australia under AUKUS.

quick.x: Nvidia chips have started switching on in Kazakhstan's US$10 billion national AI cluster, part of the global push for sovereign AI.
A former OpenAI engineer has been detained over an alleged hidden recording device in a company meeting room.

stories.h: Independent MP Helen Haines badly hurt in deliberate attack
stories.b: The member for Indi was struck twice by a LandCruiser outside her Wangaratta electorate office last Monday after the driver did a U turn. She lost a leg and remains in a critical condition at The Alfred. A local barber made a citizen's arrest and police have charged a 43 year old man. The motive is unknown.
stories.w: Leaders across every party condemned it. Haines helped create the National Anti Corruption Commission, and the attack will force a rethink of security for MPs at their electorate offices.

stories.h: One Nation is now leading some national polls
stories.b: The latest YouGov has One Nation on 27%, Labor 24% and the Coalition 23%. Newspoll from early October had Labor narrowly ahead on 29% to One Nation's 28%, with the Coalition on 20%. Albanese still leads Pauline Hanson as preferred PM, 31% to 26%.
stories.w: Australia has effectively become a three party contest on primary votes, which is historic. Chalmers has warned progressives not to mock One Nation voters, a sign Labor takes the threat seriously.

stories.b: Nationals MP Michelle Landry is retiring, opening a lower house seat that Nationals leader Matt Canavan could move into from the Senate. Earlier in the month Taylor, deputy Jane Hume and Canavan announced a migration cutting plan.
stories.w: Immigration is the main battleground with One Nation, and the Coalition is trying to win back voters on the right.

quick.x: Who's who: PM Anthony Albanese, Treasurer Jim Chalmers, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Nationals leader Matt Canavan, RBA Governor Michele Bullock.

stories.h: Inflation data this week decides the RBA's next move
stories.b: The RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.60% in September, its fourth hike this year. Since then the jobs market has turned: September lost 39,300 jobs and unemployment rose to 4.7%. September quarter CPI comes out Thursday 29 October and the RBA meets on 3 November.
stories.w: A hot CPI print with oil still high could mean a fifth hike. A soft one plus weak jobs makes a pause likely. Either way it moves mortgages, the dollar and the ASX.

stories.h: NextDC crashes 40% and AI data centres lose their shine
stories.b: Data centre operator NextDC plunged about 40% on Wednesday after returning from a trading halt linked to a dispute over power infrastructure in suburban Melbourne. Earlier, AI data centre company Firmus pulled its float after a weak investor response, and ASIC is now making inquiries.
stories.w: Investors are getting pickier about AI infrastructure that needs huge amounts of power. Grid access is becoming the bottleneck, which ties into renewables and transmission build out.

stories.h: NAB to cut up to 2,500 jobs
stories.b: National Australia Bank will shed about 6% of its workforce by mid 2027, and its shares fell on the news.
stories.w: Bank margins are under pressure and technology is replacing roles, a trend likely to spread across the big four.

stories.h: ASX says it has turned the corner
stories.b: At its annual meeting the ASX chair said the exchange had reached a turning point after years of outages and a failed tech overhaul. The regulator ordered it to hold an extra A$150 million in capital, so it cut its dividend payout to 75% of profit.
stories.w: The ASX runs the market everyone else depends on, so its reliability is a systemic issue, not just a company one.

quick.x: Japan's Daiichi Life bid $11.80 a share for wealth manager Challenger, a premium of almost 20%.
Ampol's refining margins more than doubled with oil near US$110 a barrel.
ASIC warned of cracks in private credit after property developer Bathla Group collapsed.
OpenAI's Australian arm booked $3.87 million in revenue over seven months and paid $88,000 in tax.

explainer.body: Headline CPI can be thrown around by a few volatile items like petrol or holiday prices. The trimmed mean ranks every price change in the basket, throws out the most extreme 15% at each end, and averages the middle 70%. That gives a cleaner read on underlying inflation, which is why it is the RBA's favourite number. Watch for it in Thursday's CPI release.

ahead.e: Brazil presidential runoff. Bulgaria presidential election.
US Federal Reserve rate decision (Thursday morning Aus time).
Australian September quarter CPI. ECB rate decision.
RBA decision on Melbourne Cup day. US midterm elections.
